title: Weeds behind the palace
hook: courts are splendid while fields grow weeds; this is robbery (Tao Te Ching 53)
carry: splendor that starves the fields is theft

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was seeing the small: catching things while they're still the size of a lentil. Your line was see the small.

The courtyard is swept so clean the stones shine. Silk at every shoulder. A polished sword at every hip. Long tables, and more food than anyone can finish. Now walk out past the gate, past the last wall, to the fields that feed all of this. Thistles. Nobody has worked them in a long time. And the storehouse meant for a lean winter is empty. Chapter fifty-three of the Tao Te Ching stands in that field, looks back at the shining courtyard, and gives it a blunt name.
screen: `A COURTYARD THAT SHINES.` → `PAST THE GATE: THISTLES.` → `AN EMPTY STOREHOUSE.`

segments.voice: First, the speaker's worry. The chapter opens in the first person: if I had even a little knowledge, and walked the great way, the one thing I'd fear is straying from it. Then a sigh: the great way is level and easy, and yet people love the side paths. The way isn't hard to find. It's easy to leave. Second, the picture you just walked through. The court is spotless, the fields are full of weeds, the granaries are empty. All three in one breath, so you can't look at one without the others. Third, the name. Fine robes, sharp swords, too much food and drink, wealth piled past what anyone needs. The chapter calls this robbery, the swagger of a thief, and says flatly that it is not the Tao. It doesn't call the court wicked for being clean. In one reading, the pairing is the theft: shine in the courtyard, paid for by neglect in the field. Fourth, the shape at home size. It comes in small sizes too. A budget that polishes what visitors see while what's actually needed goes without. A life that looks great online while a sick friend hasn't had a call. A company lobby with fresh flowers and a break room with a broken fridge. The question it leaves is plain: where are your fields, and what's growing in them?
screen: `THE WAY IS EASY TO LEAVE.` · `SPOTLESS COURT, WEEDY FIELDS.` · `THE PAIRING IS THE THEFT.` · `WHERE ARE YOUR FIELDS?` · then, large: `THIS IS NOT THE TAO.`

segments.voice: Walk out past your own gate in your mind: a neighbor having a hard month, a coworker stretched thin, a cause you've meant to support. Let one person or need come clearly to mind, and choose one concrete thing you could give: some money, a meal, an hour, a phone call. Hold that choice, something real and not grand, for the rest of the sit.
Weeds in the fields. Chapter fifty-three's picture: a spotless court beside weedy fields and empty granaries, which it names robbery, and not the Tao. Today's word.
Your line: splendor that starves the fields is theft. Chapter fifty-three says plainly: this is not the Tao. Go gently.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter fifty-three as a warning to anyone with means: splendor kept up while the fields and storehouses go neglected is, in the chapter's words, a kind of robbery.

notes: Editor pass: the closing question is now framed as the reader's, not the chapter's; replaced the recurring 'an ordinary Tuesday' turn.

Chapter 53 is paraphrased throughout (no Legge quotation), because the writer could not confirm Legge's exact wording. A Keeper may wish to add a verified line (e.g. on the level way and the by-ways).

The paraphrase 'if I had even a little knowledge' follows the common reading of 使我介然有知; Legge renders the opening differently ('If I were suddenly to become known...'). Confirm the paraphrase is acceptable.
'The pairing is the theft' is the writer's reading of why the chapter names the display robbery; confirm it is fair.
Original 田甚蕪 (tián shèn wú) rendered 'TYEN shun WOO'; chapter 53 has 朝甚除，田甚蕪，倉甚虛. Confirm.
The budget, social media and company lobby examples are the writer's illustrations, not the text's.
